prompt: Which goals does sustainable HRM aim to achieve according to Ehnert et al. (2016)?

options.text: Financial goals only, with social goals as a constraint

explanation: Sustainable HRM: HRM strategies and practices that enable the achievement of financial, social and ecological goals.

prompt: Which of these is NOT part of Ehnert et al.'s (2016) definition of sustainable HRM?

options.text: An impact inside and outside the organisation
Controlling for unintended side effects and negative feedback

explanation: The four elements: triple goals, inside AND outside, long term, control of side effects and negative feedback.

prompt: A firm introduces a well-being programme that also reduces turnover, but it ignores the extra workload it creates for line managers. Which element of the definition is neglected?
explanation: Sustainable HRM explicitly asks HR to control for unintended side effects and negative feedback – here, the managers' workload.

prompt: Who introduced the triple bottom line?
explanation: The triple bottom line goes back to Elkington (1997); the definition of sustainable HRM to Ehnert et al. (2016).

prompt: Which dimension of the triple bottom line covers “people & community”?
explanation: Social = people & community; ecological = environmental impact; financial = profitability & investments.

prompt: What is sustainable HRM mainly about when it uses the triple bottom line as its lens?

options.text: Maximising one dimension at a time
Managing trade-offs between the social, ecological and financial dimensions
Replacing financial goals with social ones

explanation: Many HR decisions help one dimension and hurt another – sustainable HRM makes these trade-offs explicit and manages them.

prompt: AI-based recruitment cuts hiring costs but may introduce bias against some groups. How does this show on the triple bottom line?

options.text: No trade-off – all three dimensions improve

explanation: Lower recruitment costs help the financial dimension; algorithmic bias harms the social dimension – a typical sustainability trade-off.

prompt: In the HR Director exercise, the CEO wants 12 % lower labour costs AND sustainability leadership. Which option mainly helps the financial dimension while harming the social one?

options.text: Link executive bonuses to carbon reduction and employee well-being
Introduce a living-wage commitment throughout the supply chain

explanation: Freezing recruitment and raising workloads saves labour cost (financial +) but burdens employees (social −) – it conflicts with the sustainability ambition.

basis.ref: An exercise: “You are the HR Director”

prompt: Which option from the HR Director exercise is mainly a cost-cutting move with a social downside?

options.text: Introduce a living-wage commitment throughout the supply chain
Replace some European jobs with lower-cost contractors
Link executive bonuses to carbon reduction and employee well-being

explanation: Replacing jobs with cheaper contractors cuts labour cost (financial +) but hurts employees (social −). The other three strengthen the social or ecological dimension.

basis.ref: An exercise: “You are the HR Director”

prompt: Which feature belongs to the sustainable (rather than the strategic) HRM philosophy?

options.text: HRM responsibility focuses on the own organisation
Shorter-term orientation in planning and evaluation
Responsibility also encompasses communities and other organisations
Financial performance is the most important goal

explanation: Sustainable HRM goes beyond the boundaries of the own organisation. The other three describe the strategic HRM philosophy.

prompt: How does control work in the sustainable HRM philosophy compared with strategic HRM?
explanation: Strategic HRM: top-down control. Sustainable HRM: top-down plus bottom-up.

prompt: Which of these does NOT describe the strategic HRM philosophy?

options.text: Low integration of HRM activities with business operations
Environmental, social and financial performance of equal importance

explanation: Equal importance of the three performances is the sustainable philosophy; strategic HRM puts financial performance first.

prompt: What role does the HR function play in the sustainable HRM philosophy?

options.text: A reactive function that implements decisions
A proactive and activist function that initiates, guides and sustains change
An administrative function that keeps records
An external function outsourced to consultants

explanation: Sustainable HRM: proactive & activist; initiating, guiding and sustaining change – not only implementing.

prompt: Which time orientation characterises sustainable HRM in planning and evaluation?
explanation: Sustainable HRM has a longer-term orientation; strategic HRM a shorter-term one.

prompt: Which three groups of reasons for implementing sustainable HRM do Stahl et al. (2020) distinguish?
explanation: Compliance (avoid sanctions, ethical obligations), instrumental (fit strategy, attract talent, impress investors), mission-led (do the right thing, consistency with values).

basis.ref: Reasons for sustainable HRM (Stahl et al., 2020)

prompt: A firm introduces a sustainability-oriented HR policy mainly to attract talent and impress investors. Which reason is this?
explanation: Attracting talent, impressing investors and complementing the business model are instrumental/strategic reasons.

basis.ref: Reasons for sustainable HRM (Stahl et al., 2020)

prompt: Which reasons for sustainable HRM go beyond regulations and laws according to Stahl et al. (2020)?

options.text: None – all three stay within the law

explanation: Compliance-related reasons stay within the law; instrumental and mission-led actions go beyond regulations and laws.

basis.ref: Reasons for sustainable HRM (Stahl et al., 2020)

prompt: A family firm says: “We pay a living wage because it is the right thing to do and fits who we are.” Which reason is this?
explanation: Doing the “right” thing and consistency with the company's mission and values = mission-led/values-driven.

basis.ref: Reasons for sustainable HRM (Stahl et al., 2020)

topic: Reasons for sustainable HRM – case use
prompt: Why is it useful to identify the firm's motive (compliance, instrumental, mission) in a case answer?

options.text: It decides which triple bottom line dimension matters
It tells you how far the firm is likely to go and how to sell your recommendation
It shows whether the firm is legally compliant
It replaces the analysis of trade-offs

explanation: A compliance-driven firm will do the minimum; an instrumental firm needs a business case; a mission-led firm responds to values – adapt your argument.

basis.ref: Reasons for sustainable HRM (Stahl et al., 2020)

prompt: Which practice does the lecture list under the ECOLOGICAL dimension?

options.text: Link employee green behaviour to promotional opportunities

explanation: Ecological: hire people who embrace sustainability goals, link green behaviour to promotion, eco-education. ESOPs are financial; volunteering and decent pay are social.

prompt: Under which dimension does the lecture list “integrate triple-bottom-line-based incentives in managerial compensation”?

options.text: None – it is a sin of commission

explanation: Financial dimension: ESOPs, long-term leadership development, talent retention, TBL-based incentives in managerial compensation.

prompt: Which practice does the lecture list under the SOCIAL dimension?

options.text: Eliminating child and forced labour along the supply chain

explanation: Social: volunteering, a positive work environment, health investments, no child/forced labour in the supply chain, decent pay. ESOPs and retention are financial; eco-education is ecological.

prompt: What is a “sin of omission” in HRM (Brewster & Brookes, 2024)?

options.text: HR actively contributes to a problem
HR fails to prevent a problem
HR omits a practice from Pfeffer's list

explanation: Commission = HR contributes to a problem; omission = HR fails to prevent it.

basis.ref: Sins of commission and omission (Brewster & Brookes, 2024)

prompt: Which of these is NOT a sin of commission?
explanation: Ignoring harassment is a sin of omission – HR fails to act. The others are practices HR actively uses.

basis.ref: Sins of commission and omission (Brewster & Brookes, 2024)

prompt: Which of these is NOT a sin of omission?

options.text: Layoffs purely to raise short-term profitability
Failing to develop workers whose jobs are threatened by AI

explanation: Layoffs purely for short-term profit are an active choice – a sin of commission.

basis.ref: Sins of commission and omission (Brewster & Brookes, 2024)

prompt: A firm pays its executives 300 times the median employee salary. How do Brewster & Brookes (2024) classify this?

options.text: Sin of commission – extreme executive/employee pay gaps
Sin of omission – failing to address pay inequality

explanation: Extreme executive/employee pay gaps are listed as a sin of commission: HR's pay design actively creates the problem.

basis.ref: Sins of commission and omission (Brewster & Brookes, 2024)

topic: Sins of commission and omission – case use
prompt: Why does the lecture recommend looking explicitly for sins of omission in a case?

options.text: What HR tolerates or does not do is easy to miss in a case text
They only affect the financial dimension
They are more costly than sins of commission

explanation: Practices are visible in a case; inaction (ignored harassment, unaddressed pay gaps) is not – so you have to look for it.

basis.ref: Sins of commission and omission (Brewster & Brookes, 2024)

prompt: Which statement best captures how the lecture positions sustainable HRM relative to strategic HRM?

options.text: Sustainable HRM is identical to strategic HRM with a new name
Sustainable HRM widens the scope: beyond the firm, longer-term, more integrated and proactive, with three equally important performances
Sustainable HRM drops financial performance as a goal
Sustainable HRM is only about environmental management

explanation: The lecture contrasts the two philosophies on seven points; sustainable HRM keeps financial performance but puts it on a par with social and ecological performance.

prompt: Which question is NOT among those the lecture raises when linking HRM to sustainability research?

options.text: How can HR minimise the number of employees?

explanation: The lecture asks how to define sustainability, which stakeholders are addressed, what sustainable HRM practices are, which role(s) HRM plays and how to conceptualise sustainable HRM.

prompt: A firm moves to full remote work. Its office emissions fall, but some employees feel isolated. How would you describe this on the triple bottom line?
explanation: Less commuting and office space help the ecological dimension; the social effect is mixed (flexibility vs isolation) – the lecture's brainstorm asks for exactly such trade-offs.
